summary: Children aged 7–9 learn to read fossil dinosaur trackways (trace fossils) as evidence, using a 'measure a clue → make an inference' routine: print SIZE indicates approximate body size; STRIDE (the distance from one print to the next print made by the same foot) relative to print size distinguishes walking (short stride for the print size) from running (long stride for the print size); several PARALLEL trackways in the same direction can suggest a group/herd; two CONVERGING trackways can suggest a predator following prey. Throughout, conclusions are framed as well-supported guesses, not certainties, and tracks are contrasted with body fossils to show that traces capture a moment of behaviour bones cannot. Core objective: separate the two variables — size is read from the print, speed from the spacing compared with print size — and keep reasoning qualitative (longer stride for its size = faster), not the numeric speed formula (that comes later).
misconceptions: 'Footprints show what the dinosaur looked like' — they show behaviour/movement, not anatomy.
'Wider gaps always mean a bigger dinosaur' — gap indicates speed; size is shown by print size (must separate the two).
'A trackway proves a herd/chase' — these are plausible inferences, not certainties; other explanations exist.
'The deeper/larger print means it was running' — running is inferred from long stride relative to size, not depth alone.
'Footprints and the dinosaur's bones are always found together' — tracks are usually found without the track-maker's body.

activities.title: Palaeontologist's track-reading bench
steps: Measure a single large footprint and read off an approximate, tentative body-size estimate it suggests (e.g. 'about as tall as a house'), treating that figure as a rough guide that depends on the species rather than a certainty.
Measure the stride in a trackway: the distance from one print to the next print made by the same foot.

For a fixed print size, lengthen the stride and watch a gait indicator swing from WALK toward RUN, so that speed is read from the SPACING compared with print size while size is read from the PRINT — two separate questions.

In a whole-scene mode, interpret multiple trackways: tag parallel sets as a possible herd travelling together, and two converging sets as a possible predator trailing prey, attaching your inference and how confident you are.
Respond to a 'could it be something else?' prompt by proposing an alternative explanation (e.g. parallel tracks might just be a popular path, not a herd).

Predict what the dinosaurs were doing, then watch one possible reconstruction animate them walking, running, and moving together as the tracks suggest, and compare it with your prediction, remembering the animation is an interpretation, not a recording.
activities.insight: Reading trackways is a measure-then-infer procedure: print size answers how big, stride compared with print size answers how fast, scene patterns suggest behaviour, and every conclusion is an evidence-based inference rather than a certainty.

activities.title: Annotated trackway scene: tap to reveal the reasoning
steps: Study a trackway scene and, before revealing, state what each print's size and spacing suggest.
Tap individual prints to reveal size → body-size and spacing → gait annotations, checking them against your own reading.
Tap a multi-track scene to reveal the herd and chase interpretations, then say why those are plausible rather than certain.
activities.insight: The clue→conclusion links (size→body, spacing→gait, pattern→behaviour) can be made explicit and checked, reinforcing what each measurement supports.

activities.title: Check your reading: compare and interpret trackways
steps: Given two trackways drawn to the same scale, decide which shows running and justify it from stride relative to print size.
Interpret a multi-track scene by choosing what parallel tracks might mean and what two converging sets might mean.
Use a slider to estimate 'how big was the maker?' from print size alone, keeping it separate from the speed judgement.
activities.insight: Learners can demonstrate that they read size from the print and speed from the spacing, and can offer plausible behavioural interpretations as inferences.

activities.title: Explain-your-thinking with a curious expert
steps: Present your reading of a trackway and answer probing questions such as 'How do you know it was running?' and 'Could parallel tracks mean something other than a herd?'

Work through novel cases aloud: if two trackways cross, reason about which dinosaur passed first; compare what very deep prints versus shallow prints in the same ground might tell you; decide whether a small dinosaur could ever leave widely spaced prints and when.
Revise a claim when you cannot justify it, distinguishing a well-supported inference from a guess.
activities.insight: Justifying each reading out loud and handling novel tracks strengthens the habit of treating conclusions as tentative, evidence-based inferences.

activities.title: Explore a 3D trackway site in situ (alternative)
steps: Move through a preserved three-dimensional trackway and locate a continuous line of prints.
Measure a print's size and the stride between prints in place, reading an approximate, tentative body size from the print and gait from the stride relative to size.
Interpret whether nearby parallel or converging trackways might suggest a group or a chase, framing each as a possible inference and naming an alternative.
Compare how examining tracks in a 3D setting feels against reading them on a flat bench.
activities.insight: The same measure→infer reasoning (size→body, stride→gait, pattern→behaviour) applies when tracks are examined in a three-dimensional, in-situ setting.

checkQuestion: Here are three trackways drawn to the same scale. Track A: small prints spaced close together. Track B: large prints spaced far apart. Track C: several sets of prints side by side, all heading the same way. For each track, work out what it tells you about the dinosaur — how big it was, whether it was walking or running, and whether it was alone or in a group. Talk me through your reasoning as you go.
checkAnswer: Track A: a small dinosaur, walking (small prints, short stride). Track B: a large dinosaur, running (large prints, long stride between them). Track C: several dinosaurs travelling together as a group (parallel tracks, same direction). Print SIZE indicates body size; the GAP between prints indicates speed; PARALLEL tracks indicate a herd.
